To form the gerund: hablando, comiendo, viviendo (and leyendo, durmiendo).
To say what you are doing right now: estoy + gerund.
To say what you were doing when something happened: estaba + gerund.
To say how long you’ve been doing something: llevo + time + gerund.
To say what you have just done: acabo de + infinitive; and what you are still doing: sigo + gerund.

The stress falls on “AN” / “IEN”: a-BLAN-do, ko-MYEN-do, bee-BYEN-do.
The y is read like a linked “y” sound: le-YEN-do.
Watch the changed vowel: durmiendo (not “dormiendo”), diciendo (not “deciendo”).
The Spanish gerund corresponds to the English “-ing” form: “speaking, eating, living”. It’s formed very simply:
2. ESTAR + gerund: what is happening RIGHT NOW
Just like English “I am working”, Spanish uses ESTAR + gerund for an action in progress right now. The simple present is for general facts.
Mi padre ve el fútbol los domingos.
Mi padre está viendo el fútbol.
The words that call for it: ahora, ahora mismo, en este momento, hoy (for temporary situations).
Spanish uses it LESS than English: never for the future (“I’m leaving tomorrow” = “Me voy mañana”) or for states (to know, to have, to like). “Estoy teniendo un coche” is wrong: “Tengo un coche”.
In chapter 17 you learned: “Leía cuando entró Mihai”. You can say the same thing even more clearly with ESTABA + gerund (= English “was …ing”):
I was reading (in the middle of reading) when Mihai came in.
What were you doing at eight o’clock?
We were having dinner when the phone rang.
Pronouns can be attached to the gerund or go before: “Me está enseñando” = “Está enseñándome”. Watch the accent when you attach it: enseñándome.
For “I have been doing something for… (and I still am)”, Spanish has a very handy construction with LLEVAR:
We’ve been waiting for an hour.
How long have you been living in Madrid?
The version with “hace… que”: Hace dos años que estudio español = It’s been two years since I started studying Spanish.
Don’t translate English word for word: “Estoy estudiando español por dos años” is wrong. Use “llevo… estudiando” or “hace… que”.
“Acabar de” is in the present in Spanish, but translates with “have just” in English: “Acabo de comer” = “I’ve just eaten”.
State verbs aren’t used with estar + gerund.

It’s three in the morning at the Gregorio Marañón Hospital. The city is asleep, but the hospital never sleeps.
In A&E, Mihai is working. He’s examining an elderly man with chest pains.
He’s been working for eleven hours and still has four to go.
Next to him, the nurse Pilar is bandaging a boy who fell off his bike.
Pilar has been working at this hospital for thirty years and has seen everything. While she works, she sings a song from the eighties.
In the waiting room, a mother is reading her daughter a story to calm her down. The little girl has a temperature and is crying a little.
A medical student is looking at some test results very carefully. It’s his first night shift and he’s very nervous.
Meanwhile, in Lavapiés, Ana isn’t sleeping. She’s writing the final exam for her students.
Every now and then she looks at her phone. She’s sent Mihai a message: “Are you still awake?”.
At Kenji’s restaurant, the kitchen light is still on. Kenji is making the ramen stock for tomorrow: it takes twelve hours.
At four, Mihai finally has five minutes free. He’s drinking a coffee from the machine when he sees Ana’s message.
He smiles and replies: “Yes. Saving the world, as usual. And you?”.
“Marking exams. It’s almost the same thing,” she writes.
Mihai laughs silently. Then he goes back to the ward: an ambulance has just arrived. The night goes on.
At seven in the morning, when he finally leaves the hospital, the city is starting to wake up. The bars are opening, the buses are going by and people are going to work.
Mihai yawns, smiles and thinks: “One more day.”
